heading: The four words people mix up
lede: Refugee, asylum, TPS and parole get used as if they mean the same thing. They do not. They come from different places, they last different lengths of time, and only some of them lead to a green card. If you learn one thing on this page, learn this table.

statuses.name: Refugee
statuses.plain: Approved before they ever got here.
statuses.what: Someone outside the United States who showed they were persecuted, or fear being persecuted, because of their race, religion, nationality, politics, or membership in a particular group. They are approved abroad and arrive with status already granted.
statuses.green_card_note: They must apply after one year.
statuses.lasts: Until they become a permanent resident.

statuses.name: Asylum
statuses.plain: The same protection, asked for after arriving.
statuses.what: The same standard as a refugee, but claimed from inside the United States or at the border. If they are not already in immigration court they file with USCIS. If they are in court, they raise it as a defense in front of a judge.
statuses.green_card_note: They may apply one year after being granted.
statuses.lasts: Indefinitely, until they adjust or it is taken away.

statuses.name: TPS
statuses.plain: Temporary, based on the country — not the person.
statuses.what: Temporary Protected Status. The Secretary of Homeland Security designates a whole country because of war, disaster or other extraordinary conditions. Everyone from that country who was already here and qualifies can apply. It has nothing to do with what happened to them individually.
statuses.work_note: But the work permit dies with the status.
statuses.green_card_note: It never led to one. DHS says so in writing.
statuses.lasts: 6 to 18 months at a time, and only if it is renewed.

statuses.name: Parole
statuses.plain: Permission to be here — but not an admission.
statuses.what: Temporary permission to enter or stay, given case by case for urgent humanitarian reasons. Legally it is not an admission to the country. That sounds like a technicality and is not: it decides whether someone can later apply for a green card from inside the United States.
statuses.work_note: A separate work permit application is required.
statuses.green_card_note: But it satisfies one requirement that blocks many people.

statuses.name: Permanent resident
statuses.what: Lawfully allowed to live in the United States permanently. Granted either by USCIS from inside the country, or by a consulate abroad.
statuses.lasts: Indefinitely. The card is renewed every ten years.

statuses.name: Withholding of removal
statuses.plain: Cannot be sent to that country. Gains nothing else.
statuses.what: A judge finds it more likely than not that their life or freedom would be threatened if returned. It is a higher bar than asylum and gives less: it blocks removal to that one country, and nothing more. Family members get nothing from it.
statuses.green_card_note: There is no path from here.
statuses.lasts: Indefinitely, but it is not a status.

statuses.name: Torture protection
statuses.plain: Protection from being returned to torture.
statuses.what: Under the Convention Against Torture, a judge finds it more likely than not that the person would be tortured if removed. Unlike asylum, they do not have to show it would be because of their race, religion or politics.
statuses.work_note: Depends which of the two forms was granted.
statuses.lasts: Indefinitely, though the narrower form can be revoked.

statuses.name: Work permit
statuses.what: Form I-766, the Employment Authorization Document. People often say "I have my papers" meaning this card. It only proves they may work. It is attached to some other status underneath — and when that status ends, so does the card, whatever date is printed on it.
statuses.lasts: Varies. Never longer than what it is attached to.

statuses.name: Undocumented
statuses.what: Being here without status is one thing. "Unlawful presence" is a separate clock that triggers bars on coming back: more than 180 days then leaving triggers a 3-year bar, a year or more triggers a 10-year bar. This is why leaving to "do it the right way" can lock someone out for a decade — and why nobody should decide to leave without talking to a lawyer first.
statuses.green_card_note: A waiver or an exemption may exist.
